problem_text:
A telecommunications firm must establish a fiber-optic ring network connecting seven major regional hubs:
Hub Alpha: Positioned at grid reference (172,135)
Hub Beta: Positioned at grid reference (156,25)
Hub Gamma: Positioned at grid reference (48,30)
Hub Delta: Positioned at grid reference (155,166)
Hub Epsilon: Positioned at grid reference (50,77)
Hub Zeta: Positioned at grid reference (71,176)
Hub Theta: Positioned at grid reference (46,25)

The required cable lengths between hubs, measured in kilometers, are predetermined:
Alpha to Gamma: 162.5 km
Alpha to Delta: 35.4 km
Alpha to Epsilon: 135.1 km
Alpha to Zeta: 109.0 km
Alpha to Theta: 167.3 km
Beta to Gamma: 108.1 km
Beta to Delta: 141.0 km
Beta to Epsilon: 118.1 km
Beta to Zeta: 173.3 km
Beta to Theta: 110.0 km
Gamma to Delta: 173.0 km
Gamma to Epsilon: 47.0 km
Gamma to Zeta: 147.8 km
Gamma to Theta: 5.4 km
Delta to Epsilon: 137.6 km
Delta to Zeta: 84.6 km
Delta to Theta: 178.2 km
Epsilon to Zeta: 101.2 km
Epsilon to Theta: 52.2 km
Zeta to Theta: 153.1 km

Due to a prohibitive geographical barrier, a direct cable link between Hub Alpha and Hub Beta is infeasible.
Furthermore, owing to a regulatory stipulation on shared infrastructure, the network design must incorporate exactly one of the following two cable segments: the link between Hub Beta and Hub Gamma, or the link between Hub Gamma and Hub Delta.

The objective is to determine the minimal total cable length required to construct a continuous ring network that interconnects each hub precisely once, forming a closed loop.
